units.text: Your home with a partner pulls the younger people in your life close, and that household anchors your later years.
By your late forties, you had built a home with a partner that drew in the young people around you and became the centre of your later years.
In your later years, you will find the household you make with a partner drawing the younger ones around you inside it.
Your job and your home draw on the same circle of people, a partner met through work or your parents' friends, and the line between them stays thin.
You carry the people and skills of your working life into your later years, keeping close the circle you build at work.
From your late forties, you have kept the colleagues and skills of your rising years close around your later life.
Your later life will hold on to the people and crafts of your rising years, with that working circle staying beside you.
You build your own home close to the habits of the one you grew up in, and you return to them more than you expected.
You pass the customs of your first family to the young people you raise or train, until your later years echo your earliest ones.
Since your late forties, you have handed the ways of your first family down to those who come after you, your later years mirroring your childhood.
Your later years will come to echo your earliest ones, as you hand the habits of your first home to the young ones you guide.
Your first family stays tied to your working life, with a trade or a contact or a loyalty from home going into every job you hold.
The people after you pull against the life you share with a partner, but you keep both by moving house or reworking your days.
Your work and your home compete for the same hours, and a new job or a new address follows whenever the strain grows too loud.
What you build at work in your rising years stops fitting your later life, and you change course when that chapter opens rather than hold on to it.
From your late forties, you have let go of the career your rising years built and turned toward work that fits your later life.
Your later life will outgrow the career you shape in your rising years, and when the Late Chapter opens you will change course rather than cling to it.
You make a household that breaks sharply from the home of your childhood, keeping a partner and your first family at a careful distance.
You raise or train the people after you by rules you wrote yourself, because little from the house you grew up in passes to them cleanly.
Your choice of work breaks with what your family expected, and you make your own way in a trade nobody at home chose.
From your late teens, you made your own way early and away from home, in a trade nobody in your family had chosen.
In your late teens, you will leave home early to follow work your family never pictured for you.
You, a partner and the young ones you raise or train pull together around one shared aim, your household growing stronger with each passing year.
Your work feeds straight into your household, with you and a partner backing the same plan or running something together.
Work, home and the people after you build on each other, and you keep growing what you start in your rising years through every later decade.
What you started in your rising years has grown through your Home Chapter into your later life, with work, a partner and the next generation adding to it.
You will keep building on what you begin in your rising years, as your home and the next generation add to it through each later decade.
You carry the momentum of your work well into later life, counting the people you train along the way among your strongest allies.
Since your late forties, you have carried the drive of your working years into later life, with the people you trained standing beside you as allies.
Your working momentum will carry far into your later years, with those you train turning into your closest allies.
Your first family stands behind the home you make, keeping their help close at hand while you build a household with a partner.
You bring your first family and the people who follow you together, making your own home the place where three generations meet.
You pass something your first family began to the young ones after you, adding to it alongside them through your later years.
Through your later years, you have taken up something your first family started and built on it beside the people after you.
From your late forties, you will add to something your first home started, with the people after you working beside you.
Your working life starts at a run from the household you grew up in, through doors your parents or siblings open for you.
From your late teens, you walked into openings your parents or siblings had made, the family you grew up in giving your working life a running start.
Your working life will start at a run, with parents or siblings opening its first doors for you.
Your first family, your work and your own home all serve one aim, and it gathers force as you carry it from stage to stage.
You watch one story gather weight across every part of your life, from your first home through work and partnership to the people after you.
You carry skills learned in your first home through your career into the people you train, becoming the link that passes them forward.
You spend years smoothing over a quiet friction between a partner and the younger ones in your life, the complaints nobody says out loud.
Late evenings and calls on days off wear quietly at your home life, and you guard one part of every week from your work.
Your work rubs at the people after you in small ways, a missed evening or a forgotten promise that you make up to them in person.
You settle an old irritation from your first home one small argument at a time, after it follows you into your life with a partner.
You notice a tone or a rule from your childhood rubbing at how you treat the children you raise or train, and smooth it over before it grows.
Your family never quite approves of the work you choose, a quiet doubt you answer with results more than with arguments.
You move from one chapter of your life to the next without a sharp break, because no clash, punishment or harm sits between your gates.
The same argument returns at home between you and those who follow you, but you break the loop by changing your own rule first.
You bring the standards of your work home, holding a partner to the demands you make of colleagues until you draw a line where the job stops.
You pass the pressure you put on yourself at work to the people you train, easing it once you see them repeat your hardest years.
You hear old house rules from your childhood in your own voice with a partner, and rewrite them one at a time as they come back.
You hold the people after you to the standards you were raised on, with the same friction repeating until you decide which of those rules to keep.
Your family's expectations follow you into every job, driving you harder than any boss asks until you settle on your own measure.
What you struggle with at home reappears in the people after you, and breaking the habit in yourself first keeps them from inheriting it.
You make the same mistake at work and at home, taking on too much and resenting it later, catching it sooner each time it returns.
You meet a habit that holds you back at work a second time in your later life, seeing it coming early and turning it down.
Since your late forties, you have met a habit from your working years a second time, and recognised it soon enough to turn it down.
Your later life will bring back an old working habit, and the second time around you will see it coming and turn it down.
The quarrel you grew up around repeats in your own home with a partner, and you end it by changing your own part in it.
Your childhood plays out again around the young ones in your care, and the old scene gets a different ending once you recognise it early.
You play the role you had in your family again at work, the peacemaker or the one who carries everything, and change it once you see it twice.
Because equals and money share your chart, you lose most where you share most with friends and family but keep what stays in your own name.
Your good results keep earning you a bigger role, and promotion comes on your record more than on anything you ask for.
You rise slowly and cleanly inside the places that take you in, with someone senior teaching you in each role you take on.
You turn each hard test into something you know, leaving every demanding stretch with a qualification or a title you did not have before.
Your talent argues with whoever is in charge, which costs you favour with the people who promote you and sends you to work where results count for more than rank.
Your sharpest talent has years of study behind it, which makes you known for being both daring and right.
What you make sells without much pushing, and the best pay comes from projects you would have done for nothing.
You meet pressure by making things, and a hard week ends with finished work instead of worry.
Your thinking outweighs your making, and you study a thing so long that the moment to make it passes.
